why_angle: None of the cited pages (the Dakota Powerbox 10 retailer listings, the Bixpower LF1220 pages, the Walmart and Chameleon kits) gives a measured capacity for any LiFePO4 battery. They repeat the maker's Ah and cycle ratings only. This page adds Techtest.org's electronic-load measurements: Redodo 1,378 Wh, Power Queen 1,321–1,368 Wh and ECO-Worthy 1,289–1,316 Wh against a 1,280 Wh rating, plus a one-year capacity re-test. It uses those figures to work out cost per delivered Wh with the 20A charger added.
must: pair the Redodo 12V 100Ah with Redodo's 14.6V 20A charger

page.answer: Short answer. For a LiFePO4 battery with charger, pair the Redodo 12V 100Ah with Redodo's 14.6V 20A charger: Techtest.org measured 1,378 Wh (107.7 Ah) from it, 7.7% over its rating, and the 20A charger refills it in about 5 h. Small 12V 20Ah kit with the charger included: Bixpower LF1220.

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Redodo 100Ah kit: $242.99 + $82.99 = $325.98; $325.98 ÷ 1,378 measured Wh = $0.24 per Wh delivered.
  • ECO-WORTHY 100Ah kit: $219.99 + $79.99 = $299.98; ÷ 1,289–1,316 Wh measured on its 2021 predecessor = $0.23 per Wh. That is within a cent of Redodo. Redodo gives 62–89 Wh more per charge (1,378 − 1,316 and 1,378 − 1,289).
  • Charge time on a 20 A charger: 100 Ah ÷ 20 A = 5 h at constant current. Filling the measured 107.7 Ah takes 107.7 ÷ 20 ≈ 5.4 h. ECO-WORTHY's battery page recommends a 10 A charger, which works out to 100 ÷ 10 = 10 h.
  • Bixpower LF1220: $169.95 ÷ 256 Wh = $0.66 per Wh, about 2.8× the 100Ah kits. In return the charger is in the box and it charges in 20 Ah ÷ 6 A ≈ 3.3 h.
  • Golf cart kits: Redodo $1,149.99 ÷ 5,120 Wh = $0.22 per Wh; Vatrer $1,579.99 ÷ 5,376 Wh = $0.29 per Wh.

Measured capacity: what a 12V 100Ah battery really holds

The label figure is 12.8 V × 100 Ah = 1,280 Wh. Techtest.org (Michael Barton) fully charged each battery on a 14.6 V charger and then discharged it on an electronic load until it cut out.

Battery (unit tested)Measuredvs 1,280 Wh
Redodo 12V 100Ah, standard (2022)1,379 Wh at 5 A, 1,377 Wh at 10 A, 1,378 Wh at 15 A; 107.7 Ah; 11 V cutoff+7.7%
Power Queen 12.8V 100Ah, self-heating version (2023)1,368 Wh at 5 A, 1,351 Wh at 10 A, 1,321 Wh at 20 A; about 105.5 Ah+3% to +7%
ECO-Worthy 12V 100Ah, 2021 non-Bluetooth version1,315.5 Wh at 10 A, 1,289.3 Wh at 20 A; about 101.5 Ah; 10 V cutoff+1% to +3%

After about a year of daily solar cycling, Techtest.org re-measured two of them. The Power Queen had gone from about 105 Ah to about 102 Ah (about 3% lost) and the ECO-Worthy from 102 Ah to 97 Ah (about 5% lost). Each brand was tested on one sample, and each tested unit is a sibling of the current listing rather than the exact model sold today.

The Redodo unit Techtest.org measured has no low-temperature charge cutoff, and the review counts that as a minus. Charge it above 32 °F, or choose the Low-Temp version. Redodo says that version stops charging below 32 °F and resumes above 41 °F. Redodo's 14.6 V 20 A charger uses a pre-charge, constant-current, constant-voltage cycle and can reactivate a battery whose BMS has shut it off (Redodo). LiTime explains why that matters: after an over-discharge cutoff the battery shows no output, and a charger with an activation function is what usually brings it back.

Not recommended

Dakota Lithium Powerbox 10. TackleDirect sells it for $199.00 with 10 Ah and a 3 A charger. That is $199 ÷ 120 Wh = $1.66 per Wh, 2.5× Bixpower's $0.66, for half the capacity, and both take about 3.3 h to charge (10 Ah ÷ 3 A). Its '2,000+ recharge cycles' figure comes with no depth of discharge (Inverters R Us), so it can't be compared with Redodo's 4,000 cycles at 100% DoD. Buy it only if you need its built-in USB ports, 12 V socket and lights.
